newsitem.title: ITALY: RUGBY UNION-ITALIANS IRRITATED AT OMISSION FROM FIVE NATIONS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-ITALIANS IRRITATED AT OMISSION FROM FIVE NATIONS.

text.p: Italians, still denied a place in Europe' s premier rugby union tournament, are watching with increasing irritation as this year's Five Nations' championship unfolds.
The Italian camp claims that by beating Ireland 37-29 in Dublin this January, they proved their rugby credentials on an international stage and earned the right to join the championship.
But Five Nations officials maintain Italy can not join France, England, Scotland, Ireland and Wales for at least another two years.
"The door is open and the Italians will be fully informed of the criteria," Vernon Pugh, chairman of the Five Nations committee, said recently.

For Giancarlo Dondi, newly-elected President of the Italian Rugby Federation, keeping Italy out of the Five Nations could harm the sport in a country which desperately needs international recognition if it is to build on recent success.
"Today I believe they (the Five Nations committee) think we are good enough," Dondi said in an interview. "I want to know in what sense Italy is inadequate."
Dondi said the defeat of Ireland was not a one-off victory and pointed to progress Italy had made in promoting rugby in a country where the daily sports pages are filled with little but soccer.
"Now there are 30,000 rugby players at all levels in Italy, but we hope there will be around 50,000 by the year 2000," he said.
The Italian league, until recently a holiday training ground for southern hemisphere players such as Australian winger David Campese, remains weak and under-funded.
In the recent European Cup, Italian teams Treviso and Milan fared badly, winning only one game between them in the pool stages.
Pugh has said an improvement in the domestic league is a prerequisite to Italy joining the Five Nations.

Other critics say the weakness of Italian clubs has led to an over-reliance in the national side on a few top players, such as Argentine-born fly-half Diego Dominguez, who scored 22 points against Ireland, and Australian loose forward Julian Gardner. Both are naturalised Italians.

Georges Coste, the French coach of the Italian squad, believes criticism that his side lacks strength and depth is unjust and says there is a strong pool of home-grown players waiting to take over from the current side.
"There are young players coming up. I'm quite optimistic for the future," Coste said.
"We've grown from a sporting point of view and because of that growth we deserve respect from the Five Nations."
Despite undeniable progress on the field, the fact remains that rugby in Italy is a minority sport and attracts only paltry crowds and little or no media interest.
With rugby now a big business, it seems unlikely the Five Nations will want to share profits from major sponsorships and television rights with a poorer sixth member.

Compared to the recent influx of money in the English game, the Italian league is still amateur and most top players hold down day jobs. Dominquez divides his time between an import-export business and the rugby pitch.
"We don't have the (financial) means to make the game professional here," Coste said.
Without exposure to the top international teams, and not just the likes of Portugal or Morocco, Italian match attendances and the money generated by the sport were not likely to increase, he added.

"We have to help rugby grow and for this we need contact at an international level. We need the official nature of the (Five Nations) tournament," Coste said, although adding he did not think Italy was likely to be admitted before the 1999 World Cup.
Dondi said Italy could wait two years for admittance to the Five Nations but after that it would begin to look elsewhere, possibly towards the southern hemisphere.
"We must wait, but after two years we must look for other solutions," Dondi said.
"This is a country where rugby is growing but without help it will die within three or four years."
